posts.title: Understanding JavaScript Closures
posts.excerpt: A deep dive into closures in JavaScript and how they work under the hood.
posts.content: Closures are a fundamental concept in JavaScript that allow functions to access variables from an enclosing scope, even after that scope has closed. This is particularly useful for creating private variables and functions. In this post, we will explore how closures work, with examples and practical use cases.

posts.title: JS history
posts.content: JavaScript is one of the most influential programming languages in the history of the web, shaping how users interact with websites and applications today. Its story begins in the mid-1990s, during the early days of the World Wide Web, when web pages were mostly static documents made of HTML and styled with basic CSS. In 1995, Netscape Communications was one of the leading web browser companies, with its browser Netscape Navigator dominating the market. Netscape wanted a lightweight scripting language that could run directly in the browser, allowing developers to add interactivity such as form validation, animations, and dynamic content updates. Brendan Eich, a programmer at Netscape, was tasked with creating this language. Remarkably, he designed the first version of JavaScript in just about ten days. The language was originally called Mocha, then renamed LiveScript, and finally JavaScript. The final name was largely a marketing decision, as Java was very popular at the time and Netscape wanted to ride that wave—even though JavaScript and Java are fundamentally different languages. JavaScript was first released in Netscape Navigator 2.0 in 1995. As JavaScript grew in popularity, Microsoft created its own version for Internet Explorer called JScript. This led to compatibility problems, as the same code could behave differently across browsers. To address this issue, JavaScript was standardized in 1997 by ECMA International under the name ECMAScript. This standardization helped ensure that JavaScript behaved more consistently across different environments. In the early 2000s, JavaScript was often criticized. It was seen as slow, poorly designed, and mainly useful for small scripts. However, this perception began to change with the rise of AJAX (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML). AJAX allowed web pages to update parts of their content without reloading the entire page, enabling more dynamic and responsive web applications. Popular platforms like Google Maps and Gmail demonstrated JavaScript’s true potential. A major turning point came in 2008 with the release of Google Chrome and its V8 JavaScript engine, which significantly improved JavaScript performance. Around the same time, libraries and frameworks such as jQuery made JavaScript easier to use and more accessible to developers. The language continued to evolve with major updates to the ECMAScript standard. ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) was especially important, introducing features like classes, modules, arrow functions, and promises. These improvements made JavaScript more powerful and suitable for large-scale applications. Today, JavaScript is everywhere. It runs in browsers, on servers through Node.js, on mobile devices, and even in desktop applications. From a quickly written scripting language to a core pillar of modern software development, JavaScript’s history is a story of rapid growth, adaptation, and lasting impact on the digital world.
posts.author: Robert Taylor
